podcast.body: The rhythm from Bo Diddley's song "Bo Diddley" was explicitly referenced as an inspiration for Johnny Otis's "Willie and the Hand Jive." Otis claimed to have heard the "Bo Diddley rhythm" from convicts on a chain gang before Diddley ever made a record, suggesting an independent or parallel discovery of the rhythmic pattern. "Otis coupled their expanse Han Jiving to the Bo Deadly rhythm, though he would always claim for the rest of his life, that he'd heard that rhythm from convicts on a chain gang, before Deadly ever made a record."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.body: This song is associated with the distinctive "Bo Diddley beat," a rhythm that Bo Diddley popularized and introduced to rock and roll, even though its history dates back at least 50 years before him. The beat has since been widely adopted by artists like Iggy Pop and Joan Jett. "the man who used a particular rhythm so effectively that we actually now call it the bow-diddly beat."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This song is famous for popularizing the distinctive "Bo Diddley beat," a rhythmic pattern traceable back to Yoruba Drumming from West Africa. This beat is considered non-copyrightable and has been incorporated into numerous songs across decades by various artists, including The Strangeloves, Iggy Pop, George Thorogood, and U2. "This is Bo Didley from 1955."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
